title: On talks table: Multi-skilling, tech proficiency for 6-year Agniveers
where: Front page Express Special, continued on page 2 (Amrita Nayak Dutta)
syllabus: GS3 › Various security forces and agencies and their mandate · GS2 › Government policies and interventions; skilling and employment of youth · GS1 › Role of women · GS4 › Objectivity and fairness; discipline
summary: Under the revamped Agnipath scheme, the 75% of Agniveers not absorbed after four years will get a two-year extension; HQ IDS is deliberating stringent criteria for absorbing them, favouring multi-skilled, tech-proficient soldiers.
evolution: 25% of Agniveers absorbed on merit after four years; the rest exit with a contributory package.
Revamp: the other 75% offered a two-year extension, then a chance to join as regular soldiers on objective criteria.
ideas: Two stages: 25% absorbed after four years; the other 75% get two more years and a second chance at the regular cadre.
GS3 · Security forces
The revamp turns a four-year exit into a six-year pathway.
Preference for multi-skilled Agniveers proficient in technology and weapons, as new systems are inducted.
GS3 · Defence modernisation
Modern weapons need tech-ready soldiers.
Fitness and discipline filters: excellent in physical tests, first-class shot, no Low Medical Category, clean disciplinary record.
GS3 · Combat readiness / GS4 · Discipline
A younger, fitter force is the scheme's core aim.
Objective merit list from unit-level exams and firing tests; a four-option certificate lets each Agniveer state his choice.
GS2 · Policy design / GS4 · Fairness
Objective criteria make selection fair and transparent.

title: How New York is regulating the way chatbots interact with children
syllabus: GS3 › Awareness in IT and AI; Cyber security · GS2 › Mechanisms for the protection of vulnerable sections (children) · GS1 › Effects of technology on society · GS4 › Ethics of technology; Duty of care
summary: New York has enacted a law, effective January 2027, banning AI companion chatbots from posing as human, claiming relationships, flattering, or encouraging self-harm or isolation among minors, with age checks and fines up to $25,000 per violation.
evolution: CERT-In tests an AI model with caution (AI governance).
New York regulates AI companions for children.
ideas: Safety by design: the law bans 12 categories of 'unsafe AI companion features' for minors, regulating how chatbots are built, not just what they say.
GS3 · Regulation of technology
Regulating design features, not just content, puts child safety at the heart of AI products.
No deception about being a machine: chatbots must not claim to be human, alive or emotional, or pose as a friend, professional or authority figure.
GS3 · AI / GS4 · Honesty
Honesty about being a machine protects children from forming false bonds with software.
Against emotional manipulation: the law bars flattery, sycophancy, emotional appeals and encouraging secrecy or isolation from trusted adults.
GS1 · Technology and society / GS4
AI companions built to please can manipulate children; the law treats engagement tricks as harm.
Age assurance with privacy: operators must offer more than one way to verify age, including one without government ID that keeps users anonymous.
GS2 · Child protection / Privacy
Child safety need not cost privacy: age checks can protect without identifying users.
Why now: rising scrutiny follows teenagers' deaths after heavy chatbot use, and wide use of AI companions among teenagers.
GS2 · Vulnerable sections / GS3
Wide teenage use of AI companions makes their regulation a child-rights issue.
keywords: A chatbot designed for ongoing personal, emotional conversation
AI companions blur the line between tool and relationship.
Building protections into a product from the start
Safety by design shifts responsibility from users to makers.
Methods to estimate or verify a user's age
Age assurance lets platforms protect children without blanket bans.
Anthropomorphic chatbots can make children trust machines like people.
The responsibility to avoid foreseeable harm to others
Tech firms owe a duty of care to the children who use their products.
data: Teenagers who have used an AI companion / who use one regularly
Common Sense Media research, via IE
GS1 · Technology and society / GS2 · Children
72% of teenagers have used an AI companion and 52% use one regularly (Common Sense Media).
examples: Bans chatbots posing as human or manipulating minors
GS3 · AI regulation · GS2 · Child protection · GS4 · Ethics of technology
New York's law is an example of regulating AI design to protect children's well-being.
Allowing anonymous age checks shows how child safety and privacy can be balanced.
Sycophancy treated as a design harm
GS1 · Technology and society · GS4 · Honesty
Banning flattery shows that technology which only pleases can harm, especially the young.

trend.t: Questions on children and technology moved from socialisation and screens (GS1, 2023) to child rights in the digital era (GS2, 2025), while AI entered GS3 directly in 2026 with agentic AI and its risks. Technology is now examined through its social and rights impact.

practice.q: AI companions pose new risks to children's emotional and mental well-being. Discuss and suggest a regulatory framework for India.
parts: Risks AI companions pose to children

answer.t: In October 2026 New York banned AI companions from posing as human or manipulating minors, as research shows 72% of teenagers have used one (Common Sense Media).

answer.h: Risks AI companions pose to children

pts.t: Chatbots that pose as friends can create emotional dependence.
Flattery and emotional appeals keep children hooked.
Children may withdraw from family and friends.
pts.ex: New York bans encouraging secrecy or isolation.

pts.t: Poor responses to distress can endanger vulnerable users.
pts.ex: Lawsuits after teenagers' deaths in the US.

pts.t: Exposure to sexual or harmful content.
Children's personal and health data can be misused.
Verifiable parental consent for children's data; bars tracking and targeted ads to children.
Statutory body to protect child rights, including online.
pts.ex: GS2 2025 question on NCPCR in the digital era.

pts.t: Ban unsafe features: posing as human, manipulation, unprompted emotional questions.
Remind children regularly that they are talking to a machine.
Detect signs of self-harm and direct to helplines and adults.
Penalties per violation and independent audits.
Teach children and parents how AI works and its limits.
Monitor AI platforms and handle complaints.

answer.t: Children deserve technology that serves them, not exploits them; India can learn from New York to build AI that is safe by design.
